channel.title: Nicotine Science and Policy
channel.description: Daily digest of views, debates and discussions on nicotine science, policy, regulation and advocacy.

item.title: When Tobacco Is Illicit
item.description: Illicit tobacco is what happens after policy stops accounting for demand. High taxes, restricted safer alternatives and confidence in top-down control can turn nicotine into a market run less by retailers and more by criminal networks. That weakens age checks, product standards and public oversight while keeping cigarettes cheap for those willing to buy outside the law. The lesson is uncomfortable but clear: reducing harm requires legal pathways that work better than the illicit ones. (Published on September 15, 2026byliberalism.org)

item.title: Which Oral Nicotine Products Carry the Greatest Risk? | #GFN26ScienceLab
item.description: Oral nicotine products should not be treated as a single risk category. Snus, nicotine pouches, chewing tobacco and traditional oral products can differ widely in ingredients, processing, contaminants and patterns of use. Those differences matter because public health guidance should help consumers and regulators understand where risk is actually concentrated. A clearer risk hierarchy can support better choices, stronger standards and more credible harm reduction policy. (Published on September 15, 2026bygfn.tv)

item.title: Canada Set to Loosen Nicotine Pouch Regulations?
item.description: Canada’s move to loosen nicotine pouch regulations signals a more practical turn in smoke-free policy. Keeping pouches behind excessive barriers can limit oversight, reduce adult access and leave smokers with fewer alternatives to cigarettes. A better framework would combine age controls, product standards and clear risk communication with legal routes that adults can realistically use. Regulation should make lower-risk products accountable, not invisible. (Published on September 15, 2026bydaily-pouch.com)

item.title: Five policies to get Aotearoa back on the smokefree track
item.description: Aotearoa’s smokefree goal needs policy that matches both ambition and real behaviour. Lower smoking rates will not be secured through slogans alone; they require targeted support, credible enforcement, attention to inequities and realistic alternatives for adults who still smoke. Vaping and other lower-risk options should be assessed by their role in reducing combustion, not by whether they fit an abstinence-only model. Getting back on track means focusing on outcomes: fewer cigarettes, fewer deaths and fewer communities left behind. (Published on September 15, 2026bynewsroom.co.nz)
